implementation_notes: The BCL ships the canonical realization: a decorator derives from Stream (is-a) and takes an inner Stream in its constructor (has-a), overriding the members whose behaviour changes and forwarding the rest - CryptoStream and GZipStream have exactly this shape, and the same works for any virtual interface or non-sealed class. It is the right form when the decorated object must stay substitutable for the component everywhere, including inside third-party code that only sees Stream or the interface; it is verbose because Stream has many abstract members, so every one must be forwarded deliberately. Choose the DI variant when the decorator should be applied by the container instead of at each construction site.

variants.name: Stream/interface subclass decorator (BCL shape)
variants.idiom_name: class deriving from Stream (or implementing an interface) that takes the inner instance in its constructor and delegates every member
variants.implementation_notes: The BCL ships the canonical realization: a decorator derives from Stream (is-a) and takes an inner Stream in its constructor (has-a), overriding the members whose behaviour changes and forwarding the rest - CryptoStream and GZipStream have exactly this shape, and the same works for any virtual interface or non-sealed class. It is the right form when the decorated object must stay substitutable for the component everywhere, including inside third-party code that only sees Stream or the interface; it is verbose because Stream has many abstract members, so every one must be forwarded deliberately. Choose the DI variant when the decorator should be applied by the container instead of at each construction site.
pitfalls: Stream has many abstract and virtual members (Seek, Flush, CanX, ReadAsync, Dispose): forwarding only Read/Write leaves the decoration half-applied and the async paths bypass it entirely.
Dispose ownership: a decorator that disposes its inner stream makes shared inner instances a double-dispose bug - decide explicitly whether the wrapper owns the inner resource.
Concrete-type checks (`is NetworkStream`, casts, `GetType().Name`) see the wrapper, so libraries that branch on the real stream type change behaviour once the stream is decorated.

variants.name: Dependency-injection decoration (factory registration / Scrutor Decorate)
variants.idiom_name: register the service, then register the interface with a factory that resolves the inner instance and wraps it - or Scrutor's Decorate<TService, TDecorator>()
variants.implementation_notes: In modern .NET the decorator is applied at the composition root rather than at each construction site: register the concrete service, then register the interface with a factory lambda that resolves the inner instance and returns the wrapper, so every consumer that resolves the interface gets the decorated graph. Scrutor's `Decorate` removes the factory boilerplate and wraps whatever was registered previously (including all closed generics via the `typeof(IRepository<>)` overload); the manual factory stays useful when the decorator needs extra dependencies the container should still resolve. Consumers stay unchanged because they depend on the interface, which is the point of decorating at registration time.
pitfalls: Registration order is semantic: each Decorate call wraps the previously registered implementation, so a later AddScoped silently changes the layer order, and Decorate before the inner registration throws 'required service cannot be found'.
Lifetime mismatches: a singleton decorator resolving a scoped inner service is a captive dependency that the default container only catches when scope validation is enabled.

Decorate is container-specific (Scrutor or a factory lambda) - plain Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection has no built-in decoration, so a project that avoids the extra package must write and maintain the factory wiring itself.
